pedagogy.summary: At age 13-14 children meet bivariate data: they describe the RELATIONSHIP between two variables shown on a scatter graph as positive, negative or no correlation, draw a line of best fit, and use it to make predictions. Conceptually the load-bearing ideas are three. First, correlation is about a TREND across the cloud of points — the strength is how tightly the points cluster around a line, not how steep the line is. Second, and most important, correlation is NOT causation: two variables can rise and fall together because one causes the other, because a third (confounding) variable drives both, because of reverse causation, or by coincidence — so a correlation alone never proves that changing one will change the other. Third, people tend to see the correlation they EXPECT ('illusory correlation'), over-reading a relationship when they believe a causal story and under-reading one that surprises them. Teaching should ground correlation in real, meaningful pairs (temperature vs ice-cream sales), constantly ask 'what could explain this link besides cause?', and separate strength-of-correlation from steepness-of-line.
bestPractices: Ground correlation in real bivariate contexts (temperature vs ice-cream sales, revision time vs test score) and describe the TREND in words before naming positive/negative/none
Confront correlation-vs-causation head-on with classic confounded pairs (ice-cream sales and drownings; firefighters at a fire and damage) and ask what third variable could drive both
Distinguish the STRENGTH of correlation (how closely points hug a line) from the STEEPNESS/gradient of the line — a steep line is not a strong correlation
Name the four explanations for a correlation — direct cause, common cause (confounder), reverse cause, coincidence — so 'not causation' becomes a set of alternatives, not a slogan
Read the correlation FROM the data, guarding against seeing a relationship just because one is expected (illusory correlation)
Treat 'no correlation' (no trend) as distinct from 'negative correlation' (a real, downward relationship), not as the same 'no/bad' idea
keyRepresentations: Three canonical scatter clouds side by side: positive, negative, and no correlation
A real confounded pair (ice-cream sales vs drownings) with the hidden common cause (hot weather) made explicit
Two scatters with the same gradient line but very different scatter, to separate strength from steepness
A line of best fit through a point cloud, used to read a predicted value within the data range
commonMisconceptions: Treating correlation as proof of causation — assuming that because two variables move together, one must cause the other
'Illusory correlation' — seeing or overstating a relationship because a causal link is expected, and dismissing one that isn't
Confusing the strength of correlation with the steepness of the line (thinking a steeper line means stronger correlation)
Treating negative correlation as 'no correlation' (or as 'bad'), rather than as a genuine downward relationship

learn.summary: For ages 13–14, this guidance teaches bivariate data on scatter graphs: describing the trend between two variables as positive, negative, or no correlation; drawing a line of best fit and using it to predict within the data range; and, most importantly, separating correlation from causation. Three load-bearing ideas: (1) correlation is a trend across a cloud of points, and strength means how tightly points cluster around a line, NOT how steep the line is; (2) correlation is not causation — co-variation can arise from direct cause, a common cause (confounder), reverse cause, or coincidence; (3) people tend to see the correlation they expect ('illusory correlation'), over-reading expected links and under-reading surprising ones. Activities ground every example in real, meaningful pairs and repeatedly ask 'what else could explain this link?' A live scatter sandbox with a confounder slider is the primary proposed mechanism; a Socratic sceptic, a scorable check, a static annotated gallery, and a predict-observe-explain task are preserved as distinct complementary approaches.

activities.title: Scatter sandbox: tighten the cloud, then toggle a confounder
feedback: If a learner stretches the cloud vertically so the line gets steeper and the spread grows in proportion, point out the read-out did not change: strength depends on how tightly points cluster around the line compared with the size of the trend, not on the gradient by itself.
When the temperature slider makes ice cream and drownings rise together, prompt: 'Neither of these causes the other — what is making both go up?' to surface the common cause (hot weather).
If a learner names a direct cause for a confounded pair, ask them to check whether a single third factor could be driving both before concluding one causes the other.
activities.rationale: Correlation is a felt property of a cloud of points and its trend. Manipulating the cloud and toggling a confounder may let a learner SEE strength-vs-steepness and common-cause directly, making the abstract ideas concrete. These are proposed interaction examples (live strength read-out, draggable points, temperature slider), not mandatory mechanisms; a static annotated image could illustrate the same labelled cases without live manipulation.

KS3 pupils describe simple mathematical relationships between two variables (bivariate data) in observational and experimental contexts and illustrate using scatter graphs
learnerActions: Drag points on a scatter graph and watch a live 'strength' read-out and a best-fit line update as you move them.

Stretch the whole cloud vertically (scale every y-value by the same factor) so the trend line gets steeper and the spread around it grows in proportion, and notice that the strength read-out stays the same; then pull the points closer to the line without changing its steepness and watch the strength increase.

Move a single 'temperature' slider and watch it simultaneously push ice-cream sales UP and beach-swimming/drownings UP, so a strong positive correlation appears between ice cream and drownings even though neither causes the other.
Turn the temperature slider back down and watch both variables fall together, showing that in this model, where temperature is built in as the common cause, the hidden variable drives both.

For fresh correlated pairs, use a 'what else could explain this?' prompt to name any plausible confounder, and decide which of four explanations seems most plausible for each pair, giving a reason: direct cause, common cause, reverse cause, coincidence.
activities.intendedInsight: Strength of correlation is how closely points hug the line, not how steep the line is; and a real, strong correlation can exist between two variables when a hidden third variable drives both — so correlation alone never proves causation.

activities.title: Argue it out with a sceptical scientist
feedback: If a learner accepts the causal claim, prompt them to look for a third variable that could drive both quantities.
If a learner denies any link ('they're unrelated'), affirm that the correlation is genuinely real and redirect them to explain WHY correlated things need not be causally connected.
Reward answers that name a specific plausible confounder and state that co-variation alone does not establish causation.
activities.rationale: Judging causal claims is fundamentally reasoning, and a Socratic partner can press a learner on WHY a correlation need not be cause and surface their own causal assumptions — including the expected causal stories that drive over-reading of a link. This discussion complements, and does not replace, work with actual scatter data: a conversation cannot by itself verify plotting a graph or reading a trend, so it should be paired with the data tool.
sourceClaims: 'Correlation' refers to co-variation/association between two quantitative variables and does NOT necessarily imply a cause-and-effect relationship — merely the existence of co-variation

'Illusory correlation' (Chapman & Chapman): people hold beliefs about how two variables relate that create the impression of an empirical contingency, and they overestimate the association when they believe a causal link exists between the variables
learnerActions: Respond to a character who presents tempting causal claims drawn from correlations, e.g. 'Towns with more churches have more crime — so do churches cause crime?' or 'More firefighters are sent to bigger fires and there is more damage — so should we send fewer firefighters?'
For each claim, explain in your own words what ELSE could account for the link besides one variable causing the other, and try to name the confounding common cause (e.g. town population; fire size).
When pressed, state whether the correlation is real, and separately whether the causal claim follows from it.
activities.intendedInsight: Correlation-vs-causation is an argument you can make: a real link can be explained by a confounder, reverse cause, or coincidence, so you must give a reason rather than accept the causal story.

activities.title: Predict-observe-explain: the firefighters data
feedback: A written reason of 'yes, fewer firefighters → less damage' reveals reading correlation as causation: introduce the confounder (fire size) explicitly, name the four explanations — direct cause, common cause, reverse cause, coincidence — and, if the learner has misread correlation itself, revisit what 'correlation' means (a trend/co-variation, not a cause).
A 'no, because they're unrelated' answer misses that the variables ARE genuinely correlated; affirm the real link and ask for the common cause.
A full answer names the confounder (fire size / summer weather) and states that variables moving together does not by itself establish that one causes the other.
activities.rationale: Requiring the reason BEFORE the reveal makes the task diagnostic: it distinguishes a learner who read correlation as causation from one who already holds the concept. Transfer to a fresh pair checks that the reasoning generalises rather than being memorised for one example.
sourceClaims: 'Correlation' refers to co-variation/association between two quantitative variables and does NOT necessarily imply a cause-and-effect relationship — merely the existence of co-variation
learnerActions: Study data in which the number of firefighters sent to a fire is strongly positively correlated with the amount of damage caused.

Before any discussion, WRITE your prediction and your REASON for this question: 'If the fire service sent FEWER firefighters to each fire, would there be less damage?' Commit to both prediction and reason first.
Then observe the lurking variable — the SIZE of the fire — which drives both the firefighters sent and the damage, and compare it against your written reason.
Finally, transfer the reasoning to a fresh pair: explain what could cause BOTH ice-cream sales and drownings to rise and fall together.
activities.intendedInsight: A correlation can be fully real yet not show the effect of one variable on the other, because a confounding variable (fire size; hot weather) drives both measured quantities — so changing one variable need not change the other in the way the correlation suggests (sending fewer firefighters would likely mean more damage, not less).

activities.title: Scorable check: type, strength, and causal claims
feedback: If a learner picks the steeper-but-more-scattered graph as 'stronger', show the two scatters again and point to how tightly the points hug the line, not the gradient.
If a learner labels a clear downward trend 'no correlation', contrast the three cases: positive (up together), negative (one up as the other down), none (no trend at all).
On the causal item, require the 'why' tier: a correct 'no' must be backed by a plausible confounder or other non-causal explanation, not by denying the link.
activities.rationale: Categorisation and comparison items give a scorable check, and a two-tier causal item can catch the causation misconception and the shallow-'no' error at the 'why' tier. A recognition check confirms discrimination but does not by itself elicit the independent construction of an explanation, so pair it with the predict-observe-explain and discussion tasks.
sourceClaims: 'Correlation' refers to co-variation/association between two quantitative variables and does NOT necessarily imply a cause-and-effect relationship — merely the existence of co-variation
KS3 pupils describe simple mathematical relationships between two variables (bivariate data) in observational and experimental contexts and illustrate using scatter graphs
learnerActions: Sort scatter graphs into positive, negative, or no correlation, each anchored in a real context.

Compare two scatters for strength, drawn on the same axes, including a pair where one has a steeper line but points widely scattered around it and the other a gentler line with points hugging it closely (so the gentler one clearly has the stronger correlation) — choose which shows the STRONGER correlation.
Answer a two-tier causal item: first 'Does this correlation prove X causes Y?' and then 'Why / why not?', explaining your reasoning.
activities.intendedInsight: You can reliably identify correlation type, judge strength by clustering rather than gradient, and reject an unwarranted causal claim with a stated reason.

activities.title: Annotated scatter gallery (reference)
feedback: Use the same-gradient/different-scatter pair to confirm that strength is about clustering, by revealing which is more tightly clustered.
For the confounded pair, reveal the common cause and restate that the link is real but not causal.
activities.rationale: A static annotated gallery can label the correlation types and flag a confounded pair as a reference, but it cannot let a learner manipulate the cloud or toggle a confounder to watch a spurious correlation arise. It is best used for reference and consolidation alongside the interactive and reasoning activities, not as the sole means of teaching the concept.
learnerActions: View three canonical scatter clouds side by side — positive, negative, and no correlation — and reveal each one's correlation type.
Examine a confounded pair (ice-cream sales vs drownings) and reveal the hidden common cause (hot weather).
Compare two scatters that share the same gradient line but have very different amounts of scatter, and view a line of best fit used to read a predicted value within the data range.
activities.intendedInsight: The three correlation types, the strength-vs-steepness distinction, and a worked confounded example can be recognised and named as reference points.

constraints: Ground every example in a real, meaningful bivariate pair (temperature vs ice-cream sales; revision time vs test score; firefighters vs fire damage) and describe the trend in words before naming positive/negative/none.
Treat 'no correlation' (no trend) as genuinely distinct from 'negative correlation' (a real downward relationship); do not let either be read as 'no/bad'.
Keep strength (how tightly points hug the line) separate from steepness/gradient of the line throughout; a steep line is not a strong correlation.
Frame 'not causation' as a set of alternatives — direct cause, common cause (confounder), reverse cause, coincidence — not as a slogan to recite.
When a learner misreads correlation as causation, besides naming the confounder also revisit the meaning of 'correlation' itself if needed.

The Socratic conversation cannot verify plotting or reading a trend; pair it with actual scatter data. The recognition/quiz check confirms discrimination but does not elicit independent construction of an explanation; pair it with the predict-observe-explain and discussion tasks.
The static gallery is for reference and consolidation; it cannot provide the live manipulation of cloud or confounder that may make strength-vs-steepness and spurious correlation concrete.
Line-of-best-fit predictions should stay within the data range (interpolation), as reflected in the stated evidence.

Interactive examples (live strength read-out, draggable points, temperature/confounder slider, tap-to-reveal) are illustrative proposed mechanisms, not mandatory; the same concepts can be approached with other media.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated or tested interventions, and cited claims support teaching principles rather than proving any activity's effectiveness.

The source rated a 3D interactive as adding nothing because bivariate correlation is 2D; this reflects that a third spatial dimension is not needed at this level, not an established universal claim, so it was omitted rather than asserted as a law.

The claim that live manipulation teaches strength-vs-steepness and common-cause 'in a way words cannot' was softened to a scoped affordance: the interactive may make these concrete, but a static gallery and verbal reasoning can still teach the same ideas.

sourceClaims attached to activities support the underlying principles (co-variation is not causation; illusory correlation; KS3 bivariate expectations); they do not certify that the specific sandbox, conversation, POE, or quiz designs were empirically tested. The illusory-correlation claim's attachment to the Socratic activity is a migration judgement based on that activity surfacing expected causal stories.

The illusory-correlation idea (over-reading expected links, under-reading surprising ones) is well-motivated by the Chapman & Chapman citation but is only lightly operationalised in the activities; a reviewer may wish to strengthen tasks that deliberately present a surprising-but-real correlation to test under-reading.

assess.poeTask: Show the class data in which the number of firefighters sent to a fire is strongly positively correlated with the amount of damage caused. Ask each pupil to PREDICT, writing their REASON first: 'If the fire service sent FEWER firefighters to each fire, would there be less damage?' Have them commit to prediction + reason before any discussion. THEN reveal/observe the lurking variable — the SIZE of the fire — which drives both the firefighters sent and the damage. The reason stated before the reveal is the diagnostic part: a pupil who predicted 'yes, fewer firefighters → less damage' has read the correlation as causation, while one who predicted 'no, because bigger fires cause both' already holds the concept.
probeDeeper: 'What could cause BOTH ice-cream sales and drownings to go up at the same time?' — elicits the confounding common cause
'If two things are correlated, what are all the ways that could happen besides one causing the other?' — pushes for common cause / reverse cause / coincidence
Counterexample: 'Data shows the more firefighters sent to a fire, the more damage there is — so should we send fewer firefighters? Why not?' — a fresh confounded pair (fire size)
'Here is a scatter with a steep line but points scattered all over, and here is one with a gentle line but points hugging it — which shows the stronger correlation?' — probes strength vs steepness
assess.correctAnswer: Tier 1: No. Tier 2: because correlation is not causation — a third, confounding variable (hot/summer weather) drives BOTH ice-cream sales and how many people swim (and so drown); the two are linked through a common cause, not because one causes the other. A full answer names the confounder and states that variables moving together does not by itself establish that one causes the other.

errorPatterns.pattern: Correlation implies causation: because the two variables move together, concludes that one must cause the other
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce the confounder explicitly — hot weather drives both — and name the four possible explanations for a correlation (direct cause, common cause, reverse cause, coincidence); a link is not a cause; reteach the meaning of 'correlation' via the vocabulary prerequisite
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — since ice-cream sales and drownings rise and fall together, buying more ice cream must cause more drownings
errorPatterns.revealedBy: At tier 1 the child says 'yes, more ice cream causes more drownings' (or that the correlation proves a causal link), rather than looking for another explanation

errorPatterns.pattern: Shallow 'no': denies causation but by claiming the variables are unrelated, missing that they ARE genuinely correlated (just not causally)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Affirm the correlation is real, then supply the common cause: the job is to explain WHY correlated things needn't be causally linked, not to deny the link
errorPatterns.distractor: No — ice cream and drowning have nothing to do with each other; the pattern is just a coincidence
errorPatterns.revealedBy: At tier 2 the child says 'they have nothing to do with each other', failing to explain the real co-variation via a common cause

errorPatterns.pattern: Strength confused with steepness: judges the strength of a correlation by how steep the line is rather than how closely the points cluster around it
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the two: strength is how tightly points hug the line; show two scatters with the same gradient but different scatter, and a shallow line with tight points
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a follow-up comparing two scatters the child calls the one with the steeper line 'more correlated' even though its points are more scattered

errorPatterns.pattern: Negative correlation read as 'no correlation': treats a downward relationship as the absence of correlation (or as 'bad'), not as a genuine negative relationship
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the three cases — positive (up together), negative (one up as the other down), none (no trend) — so 'negative' is a real relationship and 'none' means no trend at all
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Shown a clear downward trend the child says 'there's no correlation' because the points go down, reserving 'correlation' for upward trends

responseLevels.gap: Reads correlation as proof of causation (says the ice cream causes the drownings), or cannot describe the type of correlation on a scatter
responseLevels.full: Describes the correlation and, faced with a causal claim, rejects it by naming a plausible confounder (or reverse cause/coincidence) and explaining that co-variation alone does not establish causation — transferring the reasoning to a fresh correlated pair
responseLevels.partial: Describes positive/negative/no correlation on a scatter and may recite 'correlation isn't causation', but cannot identify the confounding common cause or explain WHY a correlation can arise without one variable causing the other — states the rule without applying it

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Pose the claim, then ask for the reason. Tier 1: 'Across the year, ice-cream sales and the number of people who drown at the beach rise and fall together — they are strongly positively correlated. Does buying more ice cream CAUSE more drownings?' Tier 2: 'Explain your reasoning — how do you account for the fact that they go up and down together?' Read it aloud and listen; do not offer options.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The two tiers together defeat guessing. A child who thinks correlation proves cause answers 'yes' at tier 1. A child who answers 'no' for a shallow reason ('they're not connected') is caught at tier 2 — they miss that the two ARE genuinely correlated, just not causally. Only a child who identifies a common cause and articulates co-variation-without-causation gives the right answer for the right reason.
